title: Welwitschia
hook: A desert plant that grows only two leaves in a life of more than a thousand years.
peek: Welwitschia lives in the Namib Desert and grows exactly two leaves, which keep lengthening from the base for its whole life. The oldest plants are thought to be well over a thousand years old.
lede: In the fog-swept Namib Desert of Namibia and southern Angola grows a plant that looks like a heap of tangled ribbons. Welwitschia mirabilis in fact has just two leaves. They never fall off. Instead they keep growing from their base for the plant's entire life, which carbon dating suggests can run past a thousand years, and perhaps far longer.

bullets.text: Each leaf grows a little every year from a strip of tissue at its base, like a slow conveyor belt. The far ends are worn by sun and sand and split into strips, which is why one plant looks like it has dozens of leaves.

The Austrian botanist Friedrich Welwitsch came across the plant in 1859 in southern Angola. He later wrote that he knelt beside it, half afraid that a touch would prove it imaginary. It was named after him.

Rain is rare in the Namib, but fog rolls in from the cold Atlantic. Welwitschia is thought to live on a mix of this fog and water drawn up by its long taproot, and it has tiny pores across both broad leaves.
The plant is a national symbol and appears on Namibia's coat of arms. In Afrikaans it is called tweeblaarkanniedood, which means roughly two leaves that cannot die.
